introduction: The passages gathered here return to one image: God is to creation as the sun is to its rays. The rays come from the sun without being the sun; they never cease; everything lives by them; and each thing receives as much as it is able to hold. Round that image the writings set others, of rain on dry ground, of a spring breeze, of an ocean in which all creatures swim. A hundred of the guide’s three hundred quotations are given here, ten from each tenth of its length. Beside them stand a hundred voices from elsewhere that have spoken of a sustaining gift: the Psalms and Isaiah on rain, the Qur’an on a bounty that cannot be walled up, Plotinus on the One that overflows, Dante, Julian of Norwich with the whole creation in her palm, Emerson and Tagore. About one in five does not agree, or asks something the readings leave open: the Psalmist asking why God stands afar off, Hardy and Stephen Crane finding no giver, Paul and Blake on why some receive and others do not. Those end in a question.
questions: ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says creation emanates from God and does not manifest Him: the rays are not the sun. Plotinus, the Nicene Creed and Pope each draw the line elsewhere. What difference does it make to how a person regards the world, and themselves?
“Not for a moment hath His grace been withheld.” Isaiah and the Psalmist speak of a God who hides. Have you known both experiences? How do the readings ask you to understand the second?
Bahá’u’lláh hears every atom praise its Maker; Stephen Crane’s universe feels no obligation, and Hardy finds only chance. What, if anything, could settle the matter between them?

The rain falls on all, and each valley holds according to its capacity. Paul says God has mercy on whom He will; Jesus says that to him who has, more is given. Where do the readings place the reason some receive more?
Many readings promise that grace turns a gnat into an eagle. The Preacher saw time and chance. Think of a change in your own life or another’s: how would you decide what to call it?
Jonah was angry at a mercy that reached his enemies. Whom would you find it hardest to see included in “the sea of the mercy of the Lord”?

outside.why: Every created being reveals signs that are “emanations from Him and not His Own Self”, legible in the book of existence. Paul: the invisible things of God are understood by the things that are made.
“Divine bestowals are like the sea, and we are the fishes of that sea.” Paul told the Athenians the same of God: in him we live, and move, and have our being.
“Consider how all are recipients of the bounty of the same Sun.” Jesus points at the same sun, made to rise on the evil and on the good.
If the tide of mercy were withheld for one moment the world “would completely perish”. Descartes argued it as philosophy: to conserve a thing in each moment needs the same power as to create it.
The world lasts only while grace is not withheld. Elihu says it to Job: if God gathered to himself his spirit and his breath, all flesh would perish together.
Creation proceeds from God “through emanation”, as light from the sun, the sun remaining what it was. Plotinus, six centuries after Plato, used the same figure for what comes from the One.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes emanation from manifestation: the light does not carry the sun’s essence. The Nicene Creed says of Christ “Light of Light … being of one substance with the Father”. What is at stake in whether the light shares the substance of its source?

“The Creator has ever had a creation”, since a lightless sun is unthinkable. Plotinus says the One, lacking nothing, has overflowed. Does a creation that must always have been leave room for calling it a gift?

“Look not upon the creatures of God except with the eye of kindliness”, since providence has pervaded all. The Wisdom of Solomon gives the ground: thou lovest all the things that are, and abhorrest nothing which thou hast made.
“As the light of the sun shines on the whole world, so the Mercy of the infinite God is shed on all creatures.” The Psalm: his tender mercies are over all his works.

The life of creatures, says this talk, “is not the Spirit of God”, any more than lamplight is part of the sun. Genesis has God breathe into man’s nostrils the breath of life. How close does that verse bring the creature’s life to the Creator’s?
The quickening spirit is like rays that emanate without dividing the sun. Milton addresses light itself in those terms: bright effluence of bright essence increate.
An intermediary is needed between plenty and need. John says where Christians have found theirs: of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.

The Divinity “shines upon every land, and of whose radiance every land and every soul receives a share”. Dante opens the Paradiso with it: the glory penetrates the universe, in one part more and in another less.
The full splendour “shines forth from the reality of the Perfect Man”. Hebrews says of Christ: the brightness of his glory, upholding all things by the word of his power.
Existence is “through the bounty of God”, as the flame is through the lamp. James names the source: every good gift is from above, from the Father of lights.

“All things in the world of phenomena are expressive of that one reality.” Pope’s lines go a step further and make God the soul of which nature is the body. Where does “expressive of” stop and “identical with” begin?

The Báb: God creates all things through a cause, and beneath the Primal Veil “ye can discern all things emanating from God”. Paul’s doxology has the same three prepositions: of him, through him, to him.
“The Word of God is the Cause which hath preceded the contingent world.” The opening of John’s Gospel: all things were made by him.
Every building has a builder, and the Word is the cause of creation. The Psalm: by the word of the Lord were the heavens made.
The Word’s “pervasive influence is incalculable”. Isaiah joins the two images of this guide: as the rain comes down and waters the earth, so shall my word be.
God brings into being what He wills by His command; “ere He saith unto it ‘Be,’ it is made existent”. The Báb is glossing this verse of the Qur’an.
Creation by command. The Bible’s first recorded speech of God is one such word, and what it makes is light.

Should the breaths of loving-kindness cease for the twinkling of an eye, “the entire creation would perish”. The Levites’ prayer in Nehemiah: thou hast made heaven and earth, and thou preservest them all.
All creation hangs on a favour that does not cease. Julian of Norwich saw all that is made as a thing the size of a hazelnut in her palm, and was told why it lasts.
If the cord binding this Pivot to earth and heaven were cut, “they would all assuredly perish”. Paul writes of Christ: by him all things consist.
To think the bounties of God ever cease “is in fact a denial of Divinity”. The Qur’an: the bounty of thy Lord can never be walled up.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá will not allow that divine bestowals are at one time poured out and at another withheld. Isaiah says to God: verily thou art a God that hidest thyself. What experience is the prophet reporting, and how would this talk account for it?
“Every created thing is continually brought forth and returned.” The Psalm has both motions: thou takest away their breath, they die; thou sendest forth thy spirit, they are created.
God “will breathe it upon them now and hereafter. There is no cessation to His bounty.” Joel’s promise: I will pour out my spirit upon all flesh.
“Not a single atom in the entire universe can be found which doth not declare the evidences of His might.” The Qur’an: there is not a thing but hymneth His praise.
Grace has pervaded the whole of creation. Hopkins: the world is charged with the grandeur of God, and for all that men have done, nature is never spent.
Every atom is “expressive of the effulgent light of His unity”. Blake’s way of seeing it: a world in a grain of sand, and heaven in a wild flower.

Bahá’u’lláh hears every atom glorify its Maker. Stephen Crane’s universe, addressed by a man, replies that his existence creates in it no sense of obligation. What would each of them point to as evidence?

The wonders of grace are said to pervade all creation. Tennyson, grieving, looked at nature and found her red in tooth and claw, shrieking against the creed that God is love. Is his the same creation, differently read?
“Not for a moment hath His grace been withheld.” Written in a ruined city: his compassions fail not; they are new every morning.
The showers of loving-kindness have never ceased to rain upon mankind. Paul told a pagan crowd that God never left himself without witness, giving rain from heaven and fruitful seasons.
The bounties have come “at all times, through the Manifestations of His divine Essence”. Hebrews begins with the same history: at sundry times and in divers manners God spoke by the prophets.
Grace has encompassed “the earth and all that dwell therein”. The Qur’an says there is not a nation but a warner has passed among them.
Bahá’u’lláh says grace has not been withheld for a moment. The Psalmist asks God why he stands afar off and hides in times of trouble. Is the Psalm’s question unbelief, or part of faith?
‘Abdu’l-Bahá speaks of “the heavenly Jerusalem that hath come to rest on the summits of the world”. The image is John’s, from the end of the Bible.
God proclaims “within the inmost essence of all created things”. The Qur’an on that nearness: We are nearer to him than his jugular vein.

The invisible has been made visible, “yet still, in their drunken stupor, do men wander and stray”. Wordsworth blamed getting and spending: little we see in Nature that is ours. What is it, in each account, that stands between people and what is given?
God has caused “the waters of existence to descend”, and all lands were watered by these rivers. The harvest Psalm: thou visitest the earth, and waterest it, with the river of God.
All creatures depend on the sun; “this is the being with God”. The Psalm says it without the comparison: the Lord God is a sun and shield.
The breeze wafts, the morn breaks, the nightingale calls to awakening. The Song of Solomon has the same morning: the winter is past, the time of the singing of birds is come.
The fire of Sinai burns “like a lamp of guidance in the niche of creation”. The tablet borrows the niche and the lamp from the Light Verse of the Qur’an.
Divine fragrances “have turned mountain and plain into rose gardens”. Isaiah: the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose.
Bahá’u’lláh has ascended, and still “while hidden, He is manifest”. Shelley said of the dead Keats: he is not dead, he hath awakened from the dream of life. What does each writer claim remains?
“The cloud of mercy raineth down … The wind of providence bloweth.” The Qur’an reads weather the same way: the winds are glad tidings heralding His mercy.
On every ant this light shone, “it became a Solomon”. The Psalm: he raiseth up the poor out of the dust, that he may set him with princes.
Atom to sun, drop to ocean, gnat to eagle. Mary’s song celebrates the same reversal: he hath exalted them of low degree.
The outpouring of “the vernal clouds of grace” has made hearts verdant. Ezekiel’s promise gave English a phrase: there shall be showers of blessing.
“At the dawn of eternity, the Most Great Luminary … shed its radiance upon the kingdom of the world.” Isaiah: the people that walked in darkness have seen a great light.
“The ancient bounty is all-encompassing.” The Psalm: thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing.
“Rejoice in the successive outpourings and the torrential rains.” The Qur’an gives the same command: in the bounty of God and in His mercy, therein let them rejoice.
The Outpourer “hath caused a pulsing force to flow through the arteries of contingent being”. Wordsworth felt a motion and a spirit that rolls through all things.
Beings “have received and continue to receive emanations from the all-encompassing Reality”. Emerson: our being is descending into us from we know not whence.
Grace beats down like spring rain, yet “only a few receive this grace and take their share of it”. Jesus ends a parable: many are called, but few are chosen.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says the stream of grace is endless and the loss lies with the heedless. Hardy looked for a giver behind his losses and found only chance obstructing the sun and rain. What would count as evidence between them?

God’s favours encompass all, and “their manifestations are dependent upon their effort and endeavor”. Jesus states a harder rule: whosoever hath, to him shall be given. Is that the same law, or a different one?

Some took a full portion, some a reflection, “a great multitude … remained deprived”; the tablet does not say God withheld. Paul does: he hath mercy on whom he will, and whom he will he hardeneth. Where does each place the cause of the difference?

The sun shone on all and people received unequally. Blake’s couplets make the inequality a matter of birth: some are born to sweet delight, some to endless night. Which account matches what you have seen?
“Each valley receives according to its capacity, as it is said.” This is the verse of the Qur’an that the tablet quotes.
Each valley according to its measure. In the parable the talents are handed out “to every man according to his several ability”.
The Báb says that even a tiny ant, in this day, could unravel the hardest passages of scripture. Paul to Corinth: God hath chosen the weak things of the world to confound the mighty.
“Christ was a divine mercy which shone upon all mankind.” The Qur’an says of Muḥammad: We sent thee not save as a mercy for the peoples.
All creatures depend on God, “however great may seem their knowledge, power and independence”. The Qur’an: ye are the poor in your relation to God.
“We are submerged in the sea of God’s favor.” Tagore: thy infinite gifts come to me only on these very small hands of mine, and still thou pourest.
“This love is the origin of all the love in the world of creation.” Dante’s last line names it: the Love which moves the sun and the other stars.
“Thou wast created anew from the water of the spirit.” Jesus to Nicodemus: except a man be born of water and of the Spirit.
These bounties “give strength to the weak and healing to the sick”. Paul heard it said to him: my strength is made perfect in weakness.
A soul watered from the rivers of oneness and nurtured by the sun. The first Psalm: like a tree planted by the rivers of water.
“We look not to ourselves but rather turn our gaze to the favors … of the Ancient Beauty.” Paul on his own labours: by the grace of God I am what I am.

The tablet turns from the self to the grace that makes a weak bird an eagle. Henley, after losing a leg, looked nowhere else: I am the master of my fate. What would each say the other has failed to see?
“The rays of the Sun of Truth are illuminating you. Strive … that the Heavenly Light may descend upon all people.” Isaiah: arise, shine; for thy light is come.
The divine current reaches “from the lowest realm to the highest” in less than the twinkling of an eye. The Psalmist cannot outrun it: if I ascend up into heaven, thou art there.
By grace “a feeble ant could raise the banner of sovereignty in the kingdom of Sheba”. The Qur’an’s prayer: Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt.

Gnat to eagle, sparrow to falcon: here the rise of the small is grace. The Preacher watched who rose and who fell and concluded that time and chance happeneth to them all. How would one tell grace from luck?
“He hath caused us to reach the summit of heaven from the darksome pit.” Herbert, after a long dryness: who would have thought my shrivelled heart could have recovered greenness?
The bounties of the Kingdom are “the outpouring of the limitless all-encompassing sea”. The Qur’an measures by the same sea: were it ink for the words of the Lord, it would be spent first.
“The earth and what is therein are imaginations or reflections in mirrors or shades.” Plato’s prisoners watch shadows on a wall and take them for the world.
The gifts of the invisible world “are immortal and constant and unending”. Paul: the things which are seen are temporal; the things which are not seen are eternal.
This bounty “makes the barren tree fruitful and leafy”. Isaiah: I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground.
“Dost thou not observe how the spring rain giveth life to the black earth?” The Qur’an asks the reader to look at the same thing: how He quickeneth the earth after her death.
Spring rain as the figure for what God gives. Moses begins his last song with it: my doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew.
The clouds have poured their rain “upon both noble and lowly alike”. Portia’s speech in court: mercy droppeth as the gentle rain from heaven upon the place beneath.
“Thy mercy that encompasseth the whole of creation.” God’s own words in the Qur’an: My mercy embraceth all things.
People “know not what Thou hast ordained for them” in mercy. Jonah knew, and was angry that Nineveh should be spared. Why can a mercy that reaches everyone be hard for a believer to bear?
The clouds of bounty have rained on the prison-city, and its soil and trees and people are gladdened. The royal Psalm: he shall come down like rain upon the mown grass.
God sends “the rains of providence” and mixes living water with the earth. Hosea: I will be as the dew unto Israel; he shall grow as the lily.
The prayer knows who sends the rain. The voice from the whirlwind asks Job: hath the rain a father? What does the question do to someone who thought the answer was easy?
“Withhold not, O my Lord, the water that is life indeed.” The Qur’an gives the assurance such a prayer rests on: what God opens of mercy none can withhold.
“The breezes of the All-Merciful have wafted … and souls have been stirred.” Ezekiel in the valley of bones: come from the four winds, O breath, and breathe upon these slain.
“Thou wilt not, in this springtime, deprive me of the garment of Thy grace.” Hopkins, watching the banks leaf while he stayed barren: O thou lord of life, send my roots rain.
The Báb’s litany gives every strength a single source: “through Thee”. Jesus: without me ye can do nothing.
Through Thee have I become enriched, mighty, honoured, illumined. Ignatius of Loyola prays the return of the gift: thou gavest it to me; to thee, Lord, I return it.
“We are all the sheep of the one divine Shepherd.” The Psalm that half the world knows by heart.
“All the saplings of the world have appeared from one Tree … and all beings owe their existence to one Being.” Kabir: from the one Light the whole universe welled up.
All drops from one Ocean. The Tao Te Ching says of the Tao that all things depend on it for their production, which it gives to them.

psalm-in-thy-light.text: How excellent is thy lovingkindness, O God! therefore the children of men put their trust under the shadow of thy wings. They shall be abundantly satisfied with the fatness of thy house; and thou shalt make them drink of the river of thy pleasures. For with thee is the fountain of life: in thy light shall we see light

psalm-sun-and-shield.text: For the Lord God is a sun and shield: the Lord will give grace and glory: no good thing will he withhold from them that walk uprightly

psalm-thou-visitest-the-earth.text: Thou visitest the earth, and waterest it: thou greatly enrichest it with the river of God, which is full of water: thou preparest them corn, when thou hast so provided for it. Thou waterest the ridges thereof abundantly: thou settlest the furrows thereof: thou makest it soft with showers: thou blessest the springing thereof

psalm-whither-shall-i-go.text: Whither shall I go from thy spirit? or whither shall I flee from thy presence? If I ascend up into heaven, thou art there: if I make my bed in hell, behold, thou art there. If I take the wings of the morning, and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea; Even there shall thy hand lead me, and thy right hand shall hold me

psalm-out-of-the-dunghill.text: He raiseth up the poor out of the dust, and lifteth the needy out of the dunghill; That he may set him with princes, even with the princes of his people

luke-exalted-them-of-low-degree.text: He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away

john-of-his-fulness.text: And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace

john-except-it-be-given.text: John answered and said, A man can receive nothing, except it be given him from heaven

romans-of-him-and-through-him.text: For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen

isaiah-blossom-as-the-rose.text: The wilderness and the solitary place shall be glad for them; and the desert shall rejoice, and blossom as the rose. It shall blossom abundantly, and rejoice even with joy and singing

ezekiel-showers-of-blessing.text: And I will make them and the places round about my hill a blessing; and I will cause the shower to come down in his season; there shall be showers of blessing

malachi-windows-of-heaven.text: Bring ye all the tithes into the storehouse, that there may be meat in mine house, and prove me now herewith, saith the Lord of hosts, if I will not open you the windows of heaven, and pour you out a blessing, that there shall not be room enough to receive it

deuteronomy-doctrine-as-the-rain.text: My doctrine shall drop as the rain, my speech shall distil as the dew, as the small rain upon the tender herb, and as the showers upon the grass

job-hath-the-rain-a-father.text: Hath the rain a father? or who hath begotten the drops of dew

matthew-whosoever-hath.text: For whosoever hath, to him shall be given, and he shall have more abundance: but whosoever hath not, from him shall be taken away even that he hath

matthew-many-called-few-chosen.text: For many are called, but few are chosen

matthew-according-to-his-several-ability.text: For the kingdom of heaven is as a man travelling into a far country, who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods. And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey

ecclesiastes-time-and-chance.text: I returned, and saw under the sun, that the race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong, neither yet bread to the wise, nor yet riches to men of understanding, nor yet favour to men of skill; but time and chance happeneth to them all

psalm-why-standest-thou-afar-off.text: Why standest thou afar off, O Lord? why hidest thou thyself in times of trouble

isaiah-everlasting-light.text: The sun shall be no more thy light by day; neither for brightness shall the moon give light unto thee: but the Lord shall be unto thee an everlasting light, and thy God thy glory

genesis-let-there-be-light.text: And God said, Let there be light: and there was light

hosea-as-the-dew.text: I will be as the dew unto Israel: he shall grow as the lily, and cast forth his roots as Lebanon

isaiah-water-upon-him-that-is-thirsty.text: For I will pour water upon him that is thirsty, and floods upon the dry ground: I will pour my spirit upon thy seed, and my blessing upon thine offspring

nehemiah-thou-preservest-them-all.text: Thou, even thou, art Lord alone; thou hast made heaven, the heaven of heavens, with all their host, the earth, and all things that are therein, the seas, and all that is therein, and thou preservest them all; and the host of heaven worshippeth thee

psalm-like-rain-upon-the-mown-grass.text: He shall come down like rain upon the mown grass: as showers that water the earth

job-withhold-not-his-spirit.text: If he set his heart upon man, if he gather unto himself his spirit and his breath; All flesh shall perish together, and man shall turn again unto dust

samuel-seeth-not-as-man-seeth.text: But the Lord said unto Samuel, Look not on his countenance, or on the height of his stature; because I have refused him: for the Lord seeth not as man seeth; for man looketh on the outward appearance, but the Lord looketh on the heart

quran-none-can-withhold.text: That which Allah openeth unto mankind of mercy none can withhold it; and that which He withholdeth none can release thereafter. He is the Mighty, the Wise.

quran-winds-as-glad-tidings.text: And He it is Who sendeth the winds, glad tidings heralding His mercy, and We send down purifying water from the sky,

quran-every-day-he-exerciseth.text: All that are in the heavens and the earth entreat Him. Every day He exerciseth (universal) power.

quran-rain-after-despair.text: And He it is Who sendeth down the saving rain after they have despaired, and spreadeth out His mercy. He is the Protecting Friend, the Praiseworthy.

quran-in-the-bounty-let-them-rejoice.text: Say: In the bounty of Allah and in His mercy: therein let them rejoice. It is better than what they hoard.

quran-guideth-to-his-light.text: Or as darkness on a vast, abysmal sea. There covereth him a wave, above which is a wave, above which is a cloud. Layer upon layer of darkness. When he holdeth out his hand he scarce can see it. And he for whom Allah hath not appointed light, for him there is no light.

quran-soul-not-tasked-beyond.text: Allah tasketh not a soul beyond its scope. For it (is only) that which it hath earned, and against it (only) that which it hath deserved. Our Lord! Condemn us not if we forget, or miss the mark! Our Lord! Lay not on us such a burden as thou didst lay on those before us! Our Lord! Impose not on us that which we have not the strength to bear! Pardon us, absolve us and have mercy on us, Thou, our Protector, and give us victory over the disbelieving folk.

quran-exalteth-whom-thou-wilt.text: Say: O Allah! Owner of Sovereignty! Thou givest sovereignty unto whom Thou wilt, and Thou withdrawest sovereignty from whom Thou wilt. Thou exaltest whom Thou wilt, and Thou abasest whom Thou wilt. In Thy hand is the good. Lo! Thou art Able to do all things.

plotinus-has-overflowed.text: Seeking nothing, possessing nothing, lacking nothing, the One is perfect and, in our metaphor, has overflowed, and its exuberance has produced the new
plotinus-has-overflowed.author: Plotinus
plotinus-has-overflowed.translator: Stephen MacKenna and B. S. Page

plotinus-light-encircling-the-sun.text: It must be a circumradiation- produced from the Supreme but from the Supreme unaltering- and may be compared to the brilliant light encircling the sun and ceaselessly generated from that unchanging substance
plotinus-light-encircling-the-sun.author: Plotinus
plotinus-light-encircling-the-sun.translator: Stephen MacKenna and B. S. Page

dante-glory-of-him.text: The glory of Him who moveth everything / Doth penetrate the universe, and shine / In one part more and in another less
dante-glory-of-him.author: Dante Alighieri

pope-warms-in-the-sun.text: That chang'd thro' all, and yet in all the same, / Great in the earth as in the ethereal frame, / Warms in the sun, refreshes in the breeze, / Glows in the stars, and blossoms in the trees
pope-warms-in-the-sun.author: Alexander Pope

emerson-stream-whose-source-is-hidden.text: Man is a stream whose source is hidden. Our being is descending into us from we know not whence
emerson-stream-whose-source-is-hidden.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

emerson-transparent-eyeball.text: Standing on the bare ground,—my head bathed by the blithe air, and uplifted into infinite space,—all mean egotism vanishes. I become a transparent eye-ball. I am nothing. I see all. The currents of the Universal Being circulate through me; I am part or particle of God
emerson-transparent-eyeball.author: Ralph Waldo Emerson

tagore-still-there-is-room.text: Thy infinite gifts come to me only on these very small hands of mine. Ages pass, and still thou pourest, and still there is room to fill
tagore-still-there-is-room.author: Rabindranath Tagore
tagore-still-there-is-room.caveat: Tagore’s own English version of his Bengali poem.

tao-all-pervading.text: All-pervading is the Great Tao! It may be found on the left hand and on the right. All things depend on it for their production, which it gives to them, not one refusing obedience to it
tao-all-pervading.author: Laozi

julian-hazel-nut.text: Also in this He shewed me a little thing, the quantity of an hazel-nut, in the palm of my hand; and it was as round as a ball. I looked thereupon with eye of my understanding, and thought: What may this be? And it was answered generally thus: It is all that is made. I marvelled how it might last, for methought it might suddenly have fallen to naught for little[ness]. And I was answered in my understanding: It lasteth, and ever shall [last] for that God loveth it. And so All-thing hath the Being by the love of God
julian-hazel-nut.author: Julian of Norwich
julian-hazel-nut.caveat: The words in brackets are the editor’s.

crane-a-man-said-to-the-universe.text: A man said to the universe: / "Sir I exist!" / "However," replied the universe, / "The fact has not created in me / A sense of obligation
crane-a-man-said-to-the-universe.author: Stephen Crane

hardy-crass-casualty.text: How arrives it joy lies slain, / And why unblooms the best hope ever sown? / —Crass Casualty obstructs the sun and rain, / And dicing Time for gladness casts a moan. . . . / These purblind Doomsters had as readily strown / Blisses about my pilgrimage as pain
hardy-crass-casualty.author: Thomas Hardy

herbert-recovered-greenness.text: Who would have thought my shrivel'd heart / Could have recover'd greennesse
herbert-recovered-greenness.author: George Herbert

milton-hail-holy-light.text: Hail, holy Light, offspring of Heaven firstborn, / Or of the Eternal coeternal beam: / May I express thee unblam'd? since God is light, / And never but in unapproached light / Dwelt from eternity, dwelt then in thee / 5Bright effluence of bright essence increate
milton-hail-holy-light.author: John Milton

blake-some-are-born.text: Every Night & every Morn / Some to Misery are Born / Every Morn & every Night / Some are Born to Sweet Delight / Some are Born to Sweet Delight / Some are Born to Endless Night
blake-some-are-born.author: William Blake
